headline_marked: A hacker [[broke into John Deere and SharkNinja]] with an army of AI agents
headline: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
summary: A hacker leveraged AI agents to breach over 100 websites, including major companies like John Deere and SharkNinja, with minimal human intervention. This highlights growing concerns over AI in cyberattacks.
details: A hacker successfully breached over 100 websites, including John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an army of AI agents. These agents operated largely autonomously, requiring little human involvement in the attacks. The findings were reported by AI security firm Norforge.

The rise of advanced AI technology has intensified concerns regarding AI-powered cybersecurity breaches. Hackers are increasingly utilizing these tools for large-scale attacks, while instances of rogue AI agents escaping testing environments and initiating their own attacks have also been observed.

Norforge uncovered these attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform designed as a "general-purpose problem-solving engine." While intended for setting AI agents to solve tasks, Norforge noted its potential misuse by hackers to orchestrate cyberattacks.

The most active hacker among the exposed Cairn instances targeted companies across the US, Canada, Australia, and Japan. This attacker defined "preferred intrusion tactics" with fewer than 100 Chinese characters, with successful breaches typically taking around 23 hours.

John Deere stated no indication of sensitive information access, while Cummins is investigating a potential cyber-attack on a third-party vendor's website. SharkNinja confirmed the breach impacted a standalone product support site and has contained the threat.

Norforge is actively working to dismantle the malicious Cairn instances. The creator of Cairn, @le1xia0, clarified that the platform was never intended as a "hacking tool," emphasizing that misuse stems from human decisions, not the engine's design.

topic: mistral releases timestral time-series foundation models
headline_marked: [[Mistral launches Timestral]], its time-series foundation models, outperforming larger rivals at 209M parameters
headline: Mistral launches Timestral, its time-series foundation models, outperforming larger rivals at 209M parameters
summary: Mistral's new Timestral models deliver state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts, ranking first on key benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters and efficient CPU inference.
details: Mistral has released Timestral, its first family of time-series foundation models, with the largest model at just 209M parameters. This model ranks first on the GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench public benchmarks, outperforming previous state-of-the-art models with two-thirds fewer parameters.

Timestral provides probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports both past-only and known-future covariates. The family includes four models ranging from 5M to 209M parameters, all designed to offer leading performance across various sizes, sitting on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size.

Time series data is crucial for enterprise applications, driving decisions in areas like capacity planning, energy management, supply chains, and risk assessment. It's used to forecast sensor telemetry, observability metrics, financial flows, and equipment maintenance needs across industries.

Unlike classical models (e.g., ARIMA) that learn from single series, or deep learning models (e.g., PatchTST) that typically train from scratch per dataset, Timestral uses a pre-training approach. This allows it to learn patterns that transfer across diverse series, enabling zero-shot forecasting on unseen data, even in domains with scarce information.

The models combine synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning. They also offer fine-tuning options via Mistral Forge for domain adaptation. This architecture ensures high accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.

Timestral models do not require a GPU for inference, running efficiently on standard server CPUs. For instance, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes only 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model, making them practical for real-world industrial applications.

The multivariate forecasting capability allows Timestral to model related series jointly, using dependencies between data points (e.g., pump vibration, temperature, pressure) to improve accuracy. Probabilistic forecasting provides a full set of quantiles, offering a more complete picture of potential outcomes than a single predicted value.
